unit.title: Suffixes with Attitude
unit.subtitle: Diminutives, augmentatives and the connotations they carry

grammar.title: It was never really about size
grammar.intro: At C2 the Spanish suffix system stops being about big and small and becomes a tool for attitude. The same ending can soften a request, drip with affection, belittle, admire or insult — and which reading applies depends on the word, the region and the tone. Learn the connotation each suffix carries, not just its literal size.

sections.heading: Diminutives: affection, softening, minimizing
sections.body: The diminutive rarely means “physically small”. -ito/-ita mainly adds warmth or softens: un momentito asks for patience, ¿un cafelito? is a cosy invitation, pobrecito drips sympathy. It can also downplay: ahorita (in a moment), un problemilla (a minor snag). Variants carry their own flavour: -illo often trivializes or turns pejorative (un abogadillo = a two-bit lawyer), while -ín and -ico are affectionate regional forms.

ex.es: Espera un momentito, que ya casi termino.
ex.en: Hold on just a sec, I'm almost done.
ex.note: softens the wait, not about time being tiny

ex.es: No es más que un abogadillo de tres al cuarto.
ex.en: He's nothing but a two-bit lawyer.

sections.heading: Augmentatives: bigness, admiration and the -azo blow
sections.body: Augmentatives amplify, but the emotional colour varies. -ón/-ona can admire or exaggerate (un caserón = a huge house, un tragón = a big eater). -azo is the star: on a noun it means admiration (un cochazo = a stunning car, un golazo = a screamer of a goal), but it also lexicalizes as a blow or sudden event (un portazo = a slammed door, un codazo = a jab with the elbow). Context decides which -azo you're hearing.

ex.es: ¡Menudo golazo ha marcado desde el centro del campo!
ex.en: What a stunner of a goal he scored from midfield!

ex.es: Se fue del despacho y pegó un portazo que retumbó.
ex.en: He left the office and slammed the door so hard it echoed.

sections.heading: Pejoratives: suffixes that sneer
sections.body: Some suffixes exist mainly to disparage. -ucho/-ucha marks something shabby (una casucha = a hovel, un cuartucho = a grotty little room). -aco/-aca and -ajo add contempt (un pajarraco = an ugly great bird, un latinajo = pretentious Latin), and -orrio/-orro makes things dreary (un villorrio = a dead-end village). These are rarely neutral — reach for them only when you mean to look down on something.

ex.es: Vivían en una casucha destartalada a las afueras.
ex.en: They lived in a run-down hovel on the outskirts.

ex.es: Se posó en la antena un pajarraco negro y enorme.
ex.en: A huge, ugly black bird landed on the aerial.

takeaways: Diminutives mostly signal affection or softening, not literal smallness: un momentito, ¿un cafelito?
-illo often trivializes or turns pejorative: un abogadillo, un problemilla.
-azo splits two ways: admiration (un golazo, un cochazo) vs. a blow/event (un portazo, un codazo).
-ucho / -aco / -orrio are pejorative by default: una casucha, un pajarraco, un villorrio.

mistakes.why: The diminutive already carries the softening; adding pequeñito is redundant and unnatural.

mistakes.w: ¡Qué cochito tan impresionante se ha comprado!
mistakes.why: Admiration for an impressive car calls for the augmentative -azo, not the diminutive.

mistakes.w: Le dio un portito a la puerta.
mistakes.r: Dio un portazo a la puerta.
mistakes.why: The sudden blow/slam is lexicalized as portazo (-azo); portito does not exist.

exercises.prompt_en: What a goal! He scored from thirty metres.
exercises.no: Admiration for a spectacular goal uses -azo: “golazo”, not a diminutive or pejorative.

exercises.prompt: No te fíes de él: no es más que un ___ que perdió su primer caso.
exercises.prompt_en: Don't trust him: he's just a two-bit lawyer who lost his first case.
exercises.no: To belittle him, use the pejorative -illo: “abogadillo”. -azo/-ón would sound admiring.

exercises.prompt: Build: “Hold on just a sec, poor thing, and have a little coffee.”
exercises.no: All three are affectionate diminutives: momentito, pobrecito, cafelito.

exercises.prompt: Salió furioso y dio un ___ que se oyó en toda la casa. (puerta + golpe)
exercises.prompt_en: He stormed out and slammed the door so hard the whole house heard it.
exercises.hint: The -azo that means 'a sudden blow', derived from puerta.
exercises.no: A door slammed shut is a “portazo” — the -azo meaning a blow/event.

exercises.prompt: Match each suffixed word to the connotation it carries.
pairs: a blow (a jab with the elbow)

exercises.tts: Vivían en una casucha a las afueras del pueblo.
accepted: vivian en una casucha a las afueras del pueblo
exercises.translation: They lived in a shabby little house on the edge of the village.
exercises.ok: ¡Correcto! “Vivían en una casucha a las afueras del pueblo.”
exercises.no: It was: “Vivían en una casucha a las afueras del pueblo.” (casucha = pejorative -ucho).

exercises.scenario: A friend shows off the sports car he just bought 🚗

lines.speaker: Diego
lines.es: Mira lo que me he comprado. ¿Qué te parece?
lines.en: Look what I've bought myself. What do you reckon?

options.text: ¡Menudo cochazo! Te ha tenido que costar una fortuna.

exercises.ok: ¡Perfecto! Para admirar un coción impresionante → cochazo.
exercises.no: To admire an impressive car you want the augmentative “cochazo”, not the diminutive or the pejorative -ucho.

exercises.say: Espera un momentito, ahora mismo voy.
exercises.en: Hold on just a sec, I'm coming right now.
exercises.ok: ¡Perfecto! El momentito suena de lo más natural.
exercises.no: Almost — tap “Hear it” and match the warm, softening tone of “un momentito”.

vocab.en: a door slam (-azo as a blow)
